title: Anchannock
summary: Anchannock / Robins Island connects colonial land transfers with Native fishing and shell-gathering rights that remained explicit in a seventeenth-century agreement.
address_label: Robins Island, Peconic Bay, Southold, NY
why_this_matters: A colonial land transfer did not necessarily erase every Native right. At Anchannock, the same agreement that assigned a settler possession of half the island protected Native fishing and shell gathering. Reading both together reveals Native presence and the competing meanings of land, water and authority behind a property record.
introduction_content: Anchannock is the recorded Native name for Robins Island in Peconic Bay. English settlers exchanged claims to the island, but a surviving agreement also protected fishing and shell gathering by Native people from Shelter Island. Its story shows why land transfers cannot be understood only as a change of owner.
history_title: Land claims, fishing rights and Native continuance
history_content:
An island between the two forks

Robins Island lies in Peconic Bay between Long Island's North and South Forks, southwest of Shelter Island and opposite the Cutchogue area. Anchannock is the Native name recorded in the 1665 deed quoted by William Wallace Tooker. His interpretation, “land well wooded,” is a historical linguistic interpretation, not a new translation supplied by today's communities.

Tooker, Indian Place-Names on Long Island (1911), entry 9, pp. 9–11.

Who claimed the land, and how?

English colonial settlers and merchants treated claims to Robins Island as interests they could transfer among themselves. A May 8, 1656 instrument, copied into the East Hampton town records, recounts an earlier transaction involving Robert Carmand and a Native sachem named Lyonancam of Pammanack. It says Carmand's claim passed to Stephen Goodyear of New Haven. These are statements in a later colonial document; they do not give us the complete earlier Native agreement or everything its participants understood.

The same record says Goodyear conveyed his claims to Roberts Island—the older English name for Robins Island—and Shelter Island on June 9, 1651 to Thomas Middleton, Thomas Rous, Constant Sylvester and Nathaniel Sylvester. The people named matter: this was a chain of specific settler transactions, not land simply becoming “colonial” on its own.

Records of the Town of East Hampton, volume I (1887), pp. 96–99.

A half-island interest tied to family lives and Atlantic trade

Another agreement, between Nathaniel Sylvester of Shelter Island and John Booth of Southold, is dated February 20, 1656 in the English Old Style calendar: February 20, 1656/57, or 1657 when the year begins in January. Sylvester agreed to give Booth possession of half of Roberts Island for the lives of Booth, his wife and child. If Booth left Long Island, the agreement required the interest to return to Sylvester with payment for specified expenses and improvements. This was not an unrestricted permanent sale of the whole island.

The contract also settled accounts involving Constant Sylvester in Barbados, goods, and debts measured in sugar. It shows how an island in Peconic Bay became entangled in settlers' Atlantic commercial dealings. The stated sugar debt was not the price of Goodyear's earlier 1651 transaction.

Records of the Town of East Hampton, volume I (1887), pp. 105–108.

Native fishing rights remained in the written agreement

The same contract required Booth to allow Native people belonging to Shelter Island to gather shells and catch other fish around Roberts Island without interference. No Native individual is named as a party signing this settler contract, but a Native community's continuing access is expressly recorded.

This is a local example of a use-right: the right to carry out particular activities in a place. It helps explain why a deed or transfer cannot automatically be read as the surrender of every relationship with land and water. The record acknowledges Native fishing while describing a settler's claim to possession. It does not tell us how consistently that protection was respected.

Records of the Town of East Hampton, volume I (1887), pp. 107–108.

What this changes about reading a deed

It would be misleading to say that Native people had no land rights, or that every agreement meant the same thing to every participant. Here, different rights appear in a single document: family possession, commercial accounts, restrictions on jurisdiction, and Native access to fish and shells. The important questions are who could exercise each right, who interpreted the paper, and whose authority could enforce it.

Read together with Shelter Island's land and plantation history, Anchannock makes the continued Native presence around Peconic Bay visible within the very records often used to describe colonial ownership. The 1665 name recorded by Tooker is another reminder that an English property name did not replace all Native relationships with this place.

Records of the Town of East Hampton, volume I (1887), pp. 96–99, 105–108.

Continuance, restoration and the limits of this map

This history raises a present-day question: what would restoring access, care and Native authority mean for the communities connected to these waters? The LandBack discussion below introduces Native-led approaches to that question. It does not claim that Robins Island has been returned or that the seventeenth-century clause establishes present-day access rights.

The island outline locates the story. It does not map the unidentified half held by Booth or a place where a document was signed. This is a private island, not a suggested walking stop; explore its history through the records and related articles.

Southold Local Waterfront Revitalization Program, Section II–J, Reach 8, pp. 18–19: island setting and access.
translation_content:
The name is interpreted Anchannock as land well wooded or full of timber, drawing on related Algonquian language comparisons. The interpretation is Tooker's historical linguistic reading rather than a settled modern translation.

Why Place Names Matter

“Replacing colonial place names with Indigenous place names does not erase history, but rather corrects it.”

— Christina Gray and Andrew Ambers, The Rematriation of Indigenous Place Names (2026), Introduction

A colonial land transfer did not necessarily erase every Native right. At Anchannock, the same agreement that assigned a settler possession of half the island protected Native fishing and shell gathering. Reading both together reveals Native presence and the competing meanings of land, water and authority behind a property record.
whereintheworld_content: The polygon follows the modern island associated with Anchannock / Robins Island in Peconic Bay, southwest of Shelter Island and opposite Cutchogue. It is an approximate geographical setting for these records, not a survey of the 1656/57 half-island interest. No dividing boundary or signing location is established by the cited text. The island's outline on the map is not permission to land on or enter private property.
